brief.head: The universal outlaw
brief.text: Ajay Shah called himself a conservative, because he never wants social engineering, and a liberal, because the world is a blank slate to rethink. {040-C15}

brief.head: A tube-light state
brief.text: Like slang’s tube light, slow on the uptake, the Indian state lags reality by ten or twenty years, Amit Varma said. Old institutions, Ajay Shah agreed, are the bottleneck. {040-C05}

brief.head: A reactor in a box
brief.text: Small modular reactors, 50-megawatt black boxes for a factory corner, could let an aluminium plant export zero-carbon metal to Europe, Ajay Shah said. Liability rules stand in the way. {040-C12}

brief.head: Never read a report
brief.text: Reports are usually boring, Ajay Shah admitted, but he called the International Energy Agency’s *World Energy Outlook 2023* unputdownable. The world of energy, he said, “is pure drama today”. {040-R01}

brief.head: The red-eye discount
brief.text: Flexible power prices work like airfares, Ajay Shah said: a red-eye or a midday flight is cheap, an 8 a.m. Bombay-Delhi flight dear, and people self-select. {#airfare}

thought.text: One should never count out the power of the human mind.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the future of electricity
lead.head: Free at noon, costly at dusk
body: Electricity, Amit Varma said, is like water to a fish: so normal that we no longer see it. So he invited listeners to dive into a plug point and travel down the wire to see what lies at the other end. {040-S01}
Ajay Shah was the guide, and the journey ran from coal plants to the price system, nuclear reactors and India’s neighbours.
His thesis: science has delivered miracles, and old institutions have not caught up.
## The old world

In the old system, Shah said, the government ran the grid. Demand from thousands of homes is smooth enough to forecast in 15-minute slots, and grid managers, like air traffic controllers, pick the cheapest plant for each.
Coal plants need a couple of hours to spin up or down, so sudden swings fall to gas and hydel. Private generators sat on 25-year contracts with fixed returns.
“It is not a world of business,” Shah said. “It is really you’re just a canteen contractor to the government.” {040-C02}

Then came what he called “miracles upon miracles upon miracles”. Solar panels have got cheaper by 20 or 25 per cent a year for 30 years. Windmills went offshore. LEDs took lighting from ten per cent efficiency to ninety.
## A cruel evening

The miracles broke the old grid. Solar floods it in the afternoon. Demand peaks in the evening, when people come home to lights, air conditioners and fridges whose compressors kick on, just as the sun goes away.
“The sun is a fickle friend,” Shah said. “He like misbehaves on you when you need him the most.” {040-J06}
Gas and hydel cannot cover the gap, and coal plants cannot be gunned all day. The planners, he said, have no good answer.
## Let prices move
Shah’s answer was the price system. “When an economist hears the word shortage, you think price,” he said. {040-C06}
Let afternoon power fall to near zero, as it already does on many summer days in Germany, and let evening power go to 15, 25 or 50 rupees a unit. Nobody, he said, should whine about profiteering.

Then three things adjust. Homes and firms shift their use to cheap hours. Wind, which blows after sunset, earns the evening premium. And storage, from batteries to water pumped uphill, becomes a business that buys cheap and sells dear.
Is that anti-poor? No, the hosts said. Without prices there are shortages, which the poor already live with, and on average power would get cheaper.

Varma’s own passion was nuclear power. Coal smoke, he read from an essay co-written by Steven Pinker, kills more than half a million people a year, while sixty years of nuclear deaths equal about one month of coal-related deaths. {040-R03}
Shah noted that India’s liability rules mean not a single American or French reactor has arrived since the Indo-US nuclear deal.

From there the wire led to Bhutan’s hydel, Nepal’s untapped hydel sites and offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. For Varma, the trip from a plug point to foreign policy was the show’s title, *Everything is Everything*, in action.
The same logic, Varma argued, could price water and parking, and even save the tiger.

second.label: A 1971 rumour
second.head: The embargo that wasn’t
second.deck: Ajay Shah ran down a story of a 1971 oil cut-off. It never happened
body: Growing up, Ajay Shah heard a vague claim: that during the Bangladesh war of 1971, the Middle Eastern states cut off India’s oil. It supposedly did not matter only because the war lasted 14 days and the Pakistani army surrendered. {#fourteenday}

The claim nagged at him. What if Saudi Arabia had been colluding with the United States? Something that big, he felt, could not be left as a vague allegation. So he reached a personal friend of an Indian ambassador to Saudi Arabia of a certain period.
The answer: it never happened. It was, Shah said, a rumour made up to portray those states as hostile to India. {040-S07} These, he said, are the ways a “toxic brew” can form.

quote.text: And I have it on full authority that no, this never happened.

second.caption: the rumoured 1971 oil cut-off

third.head: First come, first parked
body: Amit Varma owns a small car that he rather likes. Yet in Bombay he often takes an Uber or public transport, because he just won’t get parking. {#uber}

The explanation came from his friends at Takshashila. The night before recording, Varma had asked them for other uses of the price system. {040-S12} Nitin Pai said car parking: you have to price it. {#nitin}
Picture a wall, Varma said. On one side is the house, where real estate, especially rent in Mumbai, is exorbitant. On the other side is the road, where parking is free.
“It doesn’t make sense,” he said. “It means that whoever can get in there gets in there.” Need does not matter, and there are parking shortages everywhere.
third.caption: free parking in Bombay

p2.title: Follow the wire
p2.deck: Ajay Shah traces power from coal plants to Sri Lanka, and Amit Varma makes the case for nuclear

sections.label: The old world
sections.head: The grid’s canteen contractors
sections.caption: the grid’s old world
body: Before the miracles, Ajay Shah said, the grid was a government affair. Big coal, gas and hydel plants sent power at high voltage to substations, and on to every plug at 240 volts.

One household switching a TV on is random. Thousands of them cancel out, much as an insurer can predict how many car crashes it will pay for each day. “By the time you get down to any kind of geographical aggregation,” Shah said, “then cancelling out happens and there’s an insurance like character and it becomes highly predictable.” {040-C01}
So grid managers forecast demand in 15-minute slots, feeding in the weather and whether a cricket match is on, and choose the cheapest plant for each.
## Slow coal

The catch is that coal plants need a couple of hours to spin up or down. A sudden cloudy evening in Bombay must be met by gas and hydel. Amit Varma claimed to have tried it: he asked a coal plant to spin up, and “it was very slow in responding”. {040-J01}

Private generators, Shah said, were mere vendors on 25-year contracts with fixed returns, doing no thinking and taking no risk. The government did all the business thinking, and the waste came back as expensive electricity. {040-C02}
~ Meanwhile, he said, “we the fat, indolent, lazy ingrates of the world get this illusion that we just throw a switch and magically the electricity just happens.” {040-J02}

quote.text: They are brave heroic people. We value their work. It’s like an air traffic controller.

sections.label: The problem
sections.head: Sunshine at the wrong hour
sections.caption: the sun’s cruel timing
body: Climate change, Ajay Shah said, set off an explosion of research into energy, and with it a run of scientific miracles.
Solar panels have grown cheaper at a compound rate of 20 or 25 per cent a year for 30 years. {#solar}

The scientist Shockley, one of the three Bell Labs inventors of the transistor, had derived from quantum mechanics a limit on how much sunlight a silicon cell can convert. Shah remembered it as about twelve per cent. Engineers simply tried other materials and stacked them in layers. {040-S03}
## Free money from the sky

On many summer days in Germany, Shah said, the price of electricity goes to zero, and Germany does not get much sunlight. India could have 250 to 275 days of bright sun. His favourite consequence: charge your EV, and a backup battery pack, free every afternoon. {040-S06}

The catch comes at dusk. People get home and switch on lights, air conditioners and TVs, and fridge compressors kick on. Just then the sun goes away, there is not enough gas and hydel, and coal cannot spin up in time. {040-C04}
~ The renewable revolution, Shah said, had “messed with the simple boring predictable Sarkari life of the old electricity system”. Spare a thought, he urged, for the grid engineers.

quote.text: So at the worst possible time, your best possible source goes away. Like what could be more cruel than this?

sections.label: The answer
sections.head: Shortage? Think price
sections.caption: letting the price move
body: Whenever you hear “reconcile a gap between supply and demand”, Ajay Shah said, the answer is the price system. It was there “in the pages of Adam Smith in 1776”. {040-J17}

The grid engineer can only order suppliers about, because consumers pay a fixed price. Both sides should adjust. So let afternoon power fall to 25 or 50 paise a unit, sometimes zero, and let evening power climb to 15, 25 or 50 rupees a unit. {#evening}
## Three adjustments

First, demand. People would glance at the spot price on their phones before switching on the AC. Firms would work a day shift and a night shift from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., and close for the expensive evening.
Second, wind, which keeps blowing after dark. The wind investor, Shah said, would “make like a bandit in the evening when the price surge comes”. {040-C07}
Third, storage: batteries, or water pumped from the Konkan up to the Sahyadris by day and released as hydel power in the evening peak. “I’m a banya,” Shah said. “I’ll make money.”
~ None of this needs an engineer to pick the technology mix, he argued. Investors should take the risk, and go bankrupt if they guess wrong. {040-C08}

quote.text: And nobody should whine. Nobody should say those guys are profiteering.

sections.label: The nuclear option
sections.head: Sixty years, one month
sections.caption: the case for nuclear power
body: Conventional thinking on nuclear power, Amit Varma said, is “so wrong”. People think of bombs, or of Chernobyl. He read instead from a *New York Times* essay, *Nuclear Power Can Save the World*, by three authors including Steven Pinker. {040-R03}
In 60 years of nuclear power, it says, only three accidents raised public alarm. Three Mile Island killed no one. Chernobyl was the result of “extraordinary Soviet bungling”.

Sixty years of American nuclear waste would fit in one Walmart. {#walmart} France gets about 71 per cent of its electricity from nuclear, Varma said, and its carbon per kilowatt-hour is a tenth of the rest of the world’s. {#france}
## Weapons and watts

Ajay Shah drew a line. India’s nuclear journey, from Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran, was a nationalist weapons project, and that story, he said, is over. Nuclear energy should be private, competitive, global capitalism. {040-C11}
At the finance ministry, he had realised that the Kalpakkam facility, its costs reckoned correctly, was not competitive. Indian reactors were “a science project”. {040-S08}
~ Yet India holds foreign vendors liable forever for any accident. “It’s like saying I sold you a car and thirty years from now you had an accident and I’m responsible,” Shah said.

quote.text: If you care about the environment, if you care about climate change, you should embrace nuclear.

sections.label: Foreign policy
sections.head: Good neighbours, cheap power
sections.caption: power and the neighbours
body: Markets gain from larger networks, Amit Varma said, and nationalism shrinks them. Ajay Shah agreed: foreign policy is not for propaganda or scoring debating points at the United Nations, but for deals that serve the interests of the people of India. {040-C13}

Bhutan is the success. India spends military and diplomatic effort shielding it from Chinese incursions, as Doklam in 2017 showed. In return, Indian firms build and run hydel plants there, send the power home and pay Bhutan rent for the sites. {040-S10}
Nepal is the failure. Its glaciers melt in summer just as North India runs its air conditioners, but toxic fights over its constitution and a Hindu state have broken the relationship.
## Tamil Nadu’s North Sea

The third prize is offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, which Shah likened to the North Sea’s oil and gas for Britain. Electricity is a state subject, so Tamil Nadu must first build evening peak prices and markets, not flat 25-year contracts. “It is theirs to win, it is theirs to lose.” {040-S11}

~ Then India must mend ties with Sri Lanka, so Indian firms can build on Sri Lankan sites and bring the power ashore. The good Lord, Shah said, was telling both countries to “get your shit together”. {040-J12}

quote.text: There is no better deal in the world than generating Himalayan hydel electricity and sending it into the Indian Hindi heartland

sections.label: Beyond the grid
sections.head: Water, parking and tigers
sections.caption: prices in sacred places
body: Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma where else the price system solves problems in ways people don’t intuit. Varma had polled his friends at Takshashila.

Water came first. Anupam Manur, who teaches economics at Takshashila, had written about Bangalore’s water shortage and argued for pricing water. The poor are suffering anyway, Varma said, and today’s system favours the rich, who use far more of it. {040-R06}
Every interference with the price system, he argued, effectively redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich.
## Sell the tiger

His friend Barun Mitra, Varma recalled, wrote in the *New York Times*, he thought in the early 2000s, that selling tigers should be legal. People would then breed them, as they breed cows and chickens, and save the species. {040-R10}

Garbage collection could be privatised and organ sales allowed, Varma said. Shah added the makers of COVID vaccines, who he said were not paid in line with the trillions of dollars they added to world GDP, and surrogacy, where “the Indian state has come along and banned everything”. {#vaccines}
~ Agriculture and education suffer, Varma said, because the state keeps the market out of them. {040-C14}

quote.text: The answer everywhere is prices because prices are so powerful in the way that they carry information and incentives.

side.boxTitle: The fish and the plug point
side.boxText: Amit Varma opened with David Foster Wallace’s parable of a fish who asks “What’s water?” The things we normalise, he said, become unseen. Electricity is our water: we plug in, and it simply works. {040-S01}

contQuote.text: The purpose of foreign policy is to make deals with governments of other countries in the way that best suits the interests of the people of India. It is about interests.

p3.title: Tales of the grid
p3.deck: Windmills, light bulbs, an emperor and a prime minister, as the hosts told them

stories.start: Wind. Okay, you think that you put up a windmill, right?
stories.end: a uh generator attached there and you'll transport that electricity to the land
stories.caption: the windmill that kept climbing
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a simple machine went to sea
stories.head: Up, up and out to sea
body: A windmill sounds simple. How complicated can it be? You would think, Ajay Shah said, that all the genius of aeronautical engineering that figured out the propeller would do the job.

Then watch the innovations. First, engineers wanted to get off the ground, because the wind is stronger up there. Anyone who has flown a kite knows it struggles near the ground and then finds powerful winds higher up.
“Hello Viral and Vikram,” Shah said in passing, noting that you can put a dozen candles on a kite that climbs a kilometre or two.
Taller windmills needed bigger blades, which made it a problem of materials science: giant blades that are light and strong, will not break, and last 25 years. The scientists went and did that.

Then, in Shah’s telling, they grew unhappy. “I’m trapped by the surly bonds of earth. I want to go even higher. I want bigger, better, more.” So they went offshore, where the flat sea gives an even stronger wind and room for even bigger machines. {040-S04}

The next challenge was a blade about 100 metres on each side. {#blade} Steel pylons go into the seabed of India’s shallow coastal shelf, a 200-metre windmill whirs above, and the electricity is carried back to land.
~ Amit Varma later pointed out that Shah had used a Chennai slang word without knowing it: blade, meaning damn boring. Shah, he said, is the opposite of blade. {040-J03}
stories.why: Big engineering leaps, Shah’s tale suggests, come as chains of solved problems: taller towers needed bigger blades, and the hunger for more took windmills out to sea. Each answer opened the way to the next.
stories.postscript: Offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, Shah said later, is India’s North Sea. {040-S11}

stories.start: Imagine if you got to a time machine and told
stories.end: you would steal electricity, you would occasionally get bills, all that stuff would happen
stories.caption: Akbar and the light switch
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the magic we no longer notice
stories.head: Switch on, your majesty
body: Get into a time machine, Ajay Shah suggested, and visit Akbar, the most powerful ruler of the Middle Ages. Tell him you can plug something in, flick a switch, and “all kinds of magic happens”. {040-S02}
“It’s magic, okay?” Shah said. Sufficiently advanced technology, he added, is indistinguishable from magic. {040-J15}

And yet we take it for granted. We have become “dumb users”, he said: we flick a switch, the electricity flows and is metered, and a bill arrives at the end of the month. In some parts of India, he added, people steal it instead.
~ Behind the switch stand coal, gas and hydel plants, lines that carry power at high voltage to keep losses down, and substations that bring it to every plug at 240 volts.
stories.why: By the standards of history, an ordinary household commands powers no emperor ever had, and barely notices. Amit Varma made the same point with a fish that asks, “What’s water?” {040-S01}

stories.start: You would have thought Thomas Alva Edison invented the tungsten bulb
stories.end: this was exotic, expensive technology. Then it got consumerized, it got mass produced
stories.caption: the tungsten bulb
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the quiet revolution in lighting
stories.head: The bulb that was a heater
body: Ajay Shah is old enough, he said, to remember when bulbs were cool and the puzzle was making them last. Bulbs kept blowing, so their case was filled with a noble gas to stop the hot tungsten filament from oxidising.
Tube lights came next, giving the same light more efficiently. Then came the LED revolution.

“So roughly speaking in a tungsten bulb, ten percent of the energy goes out as light, ninety percent goes out as heat,” Shah said. “It’s actually a heater.” {040-S05} An LED, by contrast, reaches ninety per cent efficiency. {#led}

~ White LED light needed blue LEDs first, which Shah said great Japanese scientists at the University of California at Santa Barbara figured out. The exotic, expensive technology was then mass-produced. Today LED bulbs are everywhere in India.
stories.why: The energy revolution is not only about new ways to make power. Wasting less of it counts too: going from ten per cent efficiency to ninety was, in Shah’s words, “just miraculous gain”.

stories.start: The admiration I have for the nuclear deal that Manmohun Singh pushed through
stories.end: It is absurd, it is bizarre, it is against all rules of common sense.
stories.caption: Manmohan Singh’s stand
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a prime minister’s stand, and its sour coda
stories.head: Prime minister, or no deal
body: Amit Varma has long admired the nuclear deal that Manmohan Singh pushed through with George W. Bush. The Left parties were against it, and Sonia Gandhi did not want it. {040-S09}
Singh put his political survival at stake. “Manmohan took a firm stand and said that I will not be prime minister if I cannot do this because it’s good for the country,” Varma said.

Ajay Shah supplied the backdrop: the Indian establishment was pro-Soviet. The rapprochement with America came from leaders like Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not the bureaucracy. {#rapprochement}

~ The coda is sour. Liability rules mean not one American or French reactor has arrived since. Varma likened it to holding Hyundai liable for every accident he might ever have: “It is absurd, it is bizarre.”
stories.why: Leaders can break institutional inertia, the story suggests, but a rule further down the line can quietly undo the win. India’s liability rules, Shah said, have “negated the essence of the nuclear deal”. {#negated}

quiz.q: What limit did Shockley derive, and how did engineers get round it?
quiz.a: A cap on silicon cells’ efficiency; engineers tried other materials and stacked layers.

quiz.q: Why did Ajay Shah call the old tungsten bulb a heater?
quiz.a: Ten per cent of its energy goes out as light, ninety per cent as heat.

quiz.q: What happens to the price of electricity on many summer days in Germany?
quiz.a: It falls to zero, because there is so much solar capacity there.

quiz.q: In the Bhutan hydel deal, what does India bring and what does Bhutan get?
quiz.a: Indian firms build and run the plants and take the power; Bhutan gets rent.

quiz.q: Why does Amit Varma often take an Uber in Bombay despite owning a car?
quiz.a: Roadside parking is free, so whoever gets there first takes it, and he finds none.

quiz.q: By the essay Varma read, sixty years of nuclear deaths equal how many coal deaths?
quiz.a: About one month of coal-related deaths, even allowing for claimed Chernobyl cover-ups.
